module.title: 1 · Moment conditions
module.summary: GMM turns 'what we know about the population' into equations the data must satisfy, then minimizes how far the sample violates them.

stages.title: From assumptions to equations
stages.html:
The one big idea

Almost every estimator you know secretly says: there is some quantity in the population that should equal zero. GMM makes that statement the centerpiece.

A moment condition is a population statement of the form

E[ g(data, θ) ] = 0

where θ is the parameter we want and g is a function we choose because we believe its expectation is zero at the true θ. The vector g is called the moment function.

The simplest example: a mean

Suppose we want the population mean μ of a variable x. The defining property of the mean is that deviations average to zero:

E[ x − μ ] = 0

Here θ = μ and g(x, μ) = x − μ. That single equation is the model.

From population to sample

We cannot compute E[·], but we can compute its sample analog — the average over our n data points. Define the sample moment:

ḡ(θ) = (1/n) Σᵢ g(xᵢ, θ)

The method of moments simply sets ḡ(θ) = 0 and solves. For the mean, (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ) = 0 gives μ̂ = x̄. We just re-derived the sample average from a moment condition.

Key idea. A moment condition is a promise: "at the true parameter, this thing averages to zero." Estimation = find the θ that makes the sample version as close to zero as possible.

stages.title: When you have more equations than unknowns
stages.html:
Just-identified vs over-identified

Count things. Let θ have k parameters and let g produce m moment equations.

  • m = k (just-identified): as many equations as unknowns. You can usually solve ḡ(θ) = 0 exactly, hitting zero on the nose.
  • m > k (over-identified): more equations than unknowns. In general no θ sets all of ḡ to zero simultaneously — the equations disagree slightly because of sampling noise.
  • m < k (under-identified): too few equations; θ is not pinned down. Not usable.

The over-identified case is where GMM earns its name. We can't make every moment zero, so instead we make them collectively small. We minimize a weighted sum of squared moments:

θ̂ = argminθ ḡ(θ)′ · W · ḡ(θ)

where W is a positive-definite weighting matrix that says how much each moment (and each combination of moments) matters. This scalar quantity is the GMM objective.

Key idea. When m = k the choice of W is irrelevant (the minimum is exactly zero). When m > k, W matters — and choosing it well is the whole game in Module 4.

Notice this nests the method of moments: if you can drive ḡ to zero, then ḡ′Wḡ = 0 for any W, so the GMM solution coincides with the exact solution.

stages.title: Hand-roll GMM for a mean
stages.note: Estimate μ from the single moment E[x−μ]=0 by literally minimizing the GMM objective with scipy. With one moment and one parameter (m=k=1) the objective is driven to zero and μ̂ equals the sample mean.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(5.0, 2.0, n)   # true mean 5

# moment function g(x, mu) = x - mu  ->  sample moment is its average
def gbar(mu):
    return np.array([np.mean(x - mu)])

# GMM objective  J(mu) = gbar' W gbar,  here W = 1 (scalar, m=1)
def objective(p):
    g = gbar(p[0])
    return float(g @ g)

res = minimize(objective, x0=[0.0])
mu_hat = res.x[0]

print(f'sample mean x̄        = {x.mean():.6f}')
print(f'GMM μ̂ (minimizer)    = {mu_hat:.6f}')
print(f'objective at optimum  = {objective([mu_hat]):.3e}  (≈ 0, just-identified)')
print(f'gbar at optimum       = {gbar(mu_hat)[0]:.3e}')

stages.title: Watch the GMM objective J(μ)
stages.note: The objective ḡ(μ)′ḡ(μ) is a parabola in μ that bottoms out exactly at the sample mean. Drag the candidate μ and read off J. The orange marker is your guess; the dashed line is where J is minimized (the sample mean).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(5.0, 2.0, n)
def J(mu):
    g = np.mean(x - mu)
    return g*g
grid = np.linspace(0,10,200)
vals = [J(m) for m in grid]
mu_star = x.mean()
mu = {{mu}}
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(grid, vals, color='#af983f', lw=2, label='J(μ)=ḡ(μ)²')
plt.axvline(mu_star, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=1.5, label=f'min at x̄={mu_star:.2f}')
plt.scatter([mu],[J(mu)], color='#da9100', s=70, zorder=5, label='your μ')
plt.xlabel('candidate μ'); plt.ylabel('GMM objective J')
plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'μ={mu:.2f}  →  J={J(mu):.4f}   (min J at μ={mu_star:.2f})')

stages.title: Check: counting moments
stages.prompt: You have a model with 2 parameters and you write down 5 moment conditions. This model is:
choices: under-identified, so GMM cannot be used
just-identified, so the weighting matrix is irrelevant
over-identified, so GMM minimizes a weighted sum of moments and W matters
exactly-identified only if the moments are independent
stages.hint: Compare m (number of moments) with k (number of parameters).
stages.explain: With m = 5 moments and k = 2 parameters, m > k: the model is over-identified. You generally can't zero out all moments at once, so GMM minimizes ḡ′Wḡ and the choice of W changes the estimate.

stages.title: Check: what is a moment condition?
stages.prompt: The moment condition E[x − μ] = 0 is used to estimate μ. What does the sample analog (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ̂) = 0 give you?
choices: an arbitrary value depending on W
stages.explain: Setting the sample moment to zero gives Σxᵢ = nμ̂, i.e. μ̂ = x̄. The method-of-moments estimator of the mean is just the sample average.

stages.title: Counting the surplus
stages.prompt: When you write down more moment conditions than parameters (m > k), the model is said to be ___.
stages.lead: You just saw a model with 5 moment conditions for 2 parameters — there are more equations than unknowns.
stages.hint: It's the opposite of 'just-identified' (m = k). The prefix means you have a surplus.
stages.explain: The 'extra moments are wasted' instinct, named: a model with m > k is over-identified, and those surplus moments are not wasted — they give you a testable restriction (the J-test) and, if valid, extra efficiency. The tempting belief is that you should always reduce to m = k so every moment binds exactly; that throws away the over-identifying information. Boundary: exactly m = k is just-identified (moments hit zero exactly, W is irrelevant); m < k is under-identified and not estimable.

stages.title: How many over-identifying restrictions?
stages.prompt: A GMM model has m = 5 moment conditions and k = 2 parameters. How many over-identifying restrictions does it have? (enter a whole number)
stages.hint: Over-identifying restrictions = surplus moments = m − k.
stages.explain: The 'restrictions = number of moments' trap: the count of over-identifying restrictions is m − k = 5 − 2 = 3, not 5. The tempting answer 5 counts all moments; but k of them are 'spent' pinning down the k parameters, leaving only m − k as independent checks. Boundary: when m = k the count is 0 — a just-identified model has nothing left over to test, which is exactly why no J-test exists there.
